name: stat
plain: `stat` shows everything the file system knows about a file apart from its contents: exact size, permissions, owner, inode number, link count and four timestamps.
The timestamps matter in forensics: Access (read), Modify (content changed), Change (metadata changed, e.g. permissions or rename) and Birth (created, where supported).
when: See exact permissions in octal and who owns a file.
Check a file's size in bytes.
Check whether two names are hard links to the same file (same inode).

examples.title: Everything about a file
examples.explain: Shows size, blocks, inode, links, permissions (numeric and symbolic), uid/gid, and Access, Modify, Change and Birth times.

examples.title: Just the permissions and name
examples.explain: -c sets a format: %a octal permissions, %U owner, %G group, %n name. One compact line per file.

examples.title: Size in bytes
examples.explain: %s is the size in bytes, ready for scripts.

examples.title: Modification time as epoch
examples.explain: %Y is the Unix timestamp of last modification; sorting gives a quick timeline.

examples.title: Readable modification time
examples.explain: %y is the modification time in human form.

examples.title: File system details
examples.explain: -f describes the file system (block size, free blocks, type).

examples.title: Follow a symlink
examples.explain: -L shows the target's information instead of the link's.

options.plain: Use a format string (%n name, %s size, %a/%A permissions, %U/%G owner/group, %i inode, %h hard links, %x/%y/%z/%w atime/mtime/ctime/birth, %X/%Y/%Z/%W as epoch, %F type).
Like -c but interprets backslash escapes and adds no newline.
Show file system status instead of file status.
Control caching of attributes on network file systems.

mistakes: Treating access time as exact: many systems relax it, so it may not change on every read.
Believing Change time is creation time: it is the last metadata change.
Forgetting -L for symlinks and reading the link's own information.
Birth time shown as '-': the file system does not record it.
try: Run stat on a file, touch it, then stat again and see which times changed.
Run chmod on it and watch Change.
List a folder sorted by modification epoch.
see_also: ls(1), find(1), file(1), touch(1), chmod(1), date(1), debugfs(8).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
